title: Supervised Classification Heads as Semantic Prototypes: Unlocking Vision-Language Alignment via Weight Recycling
one_liner: Reuse the class-label weights already learned by a vision model as semantic reference points, then use them to align images and text with much less paired data.
lead: Vision-language alignment usually depends on large image-text datasets because the model must learn how visual features and text features refer to the same concepts. This paper asks whether a vision model already contains part of that alignment signal in a neglected place: the supervised classification head. A classification head is the final layer whose weight vectors, meaning lists of numbers that define one class direction each, point toward classes such as dog, car, or tree. Those weight vectors are usually discarded after pretraining. The paper argues that they can act as semantic prototypes, meaning reference directions associated with recognizable concepts, and that reusing them can support both zero-shot alignment and data augmentation for post-hoc alignment methods.

problem.h2: Why post-hoc alignment still needs a lot of paired data
paras: Suppose you already have a strong vision encoder and a strong text encoder. A post-hoc alignment method tries to connect them after the fact, usually by learning a small mapping between their feature spaces. That is cheaper than training a full vision-language model from scratch, but it still needs many paired image-text examples because the mapping has to discover what concepts correspond across modalities.

The paper points out that a supervised vision model has already learned a semantic structure during classification training. To separate classes, the final weight vectors must encode directions that correspond to concrete visual concepts. Throwing those vectors away means discarding concept anchors that could help alignment from the start because they already summarize how the vision encoder separates classes.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Treat the vision classifier's output weights as reusable semantic prototypes and inject them into alignment, because those weights already summarize class-level concept structure.

steps.text: Start with a model trained for supervised image classification so its final class-head weights already encode class separation.
Use each weight vector as a semantic prototype, meaning a representative direction for one class concept in feature space.
Connect text features to those prototype directions so alignment can begin even before many paired image-text examples are available.
Mix prototype-based supervision with real image-text pairs because the prototypes add extra concept-level constraints.
Combine this recycling step with existing lightweight alignment methods rather than replacing them.

paras: The paper changes what information is preserved from supervised vision pretraining. It keeps the classification head and repurposes its weights as explicit semantic anchors for later cross-modal alignment.

hidden.name: Concept prototype quality
paras: The key hidden quantity is how well a classifier-head weight vector really represents a semantic concept beyond the narrow original classification task. That quality is not directly labeled. You only observe downstream alignment performance after reusing the weights.

The paper bets that these vectors are useful prototypes because classification training pushes them to respond strongly to one concept and weakly to competing concepts. If that structure transfers, then the vectors can anchor both image features and text features around shared concept directions.

heat.caption: Darker cells indicate the properties that make a recycled class weight a useful semantic prototype.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is whether a class-head weight is a clean concept reference point or only a task-specific learned number pattern.
Weight recycling assumes classifier-head vectors encode reusable semantic structure that can serve as anchors for aligning image and text representations.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: classifier heads already contain concept structure
paras: In supervised classification, the final weight vector for a class must score examples of that class higher than alternatives. To do that, the encoder and head co-adapt so that images of one class gather around directions favored by the corresponding weight vector. That means the head is not an arbitrary output layer. It is part of the learned concept structure, meaning the arrangement of concept directions in feature space.

If those directions are kept, they can serve as semantic anchors during multimodal alignment. A text encoder that maps the phrase for a class toward the same direction gains an immediate concept-level reference. This helps in low-data settings because the alignment method no longer starts from an unconstrained relation between image and text spaces.

The augmentation role follows from the same idea. Prototype-based mixed pairs inject additional semantic supervision beyond the limited real pairs. That helps because the aligner sees not only isolated examples but also explicit class-centered reference directions that organize the training signal.

stages.s: pretrained vision encoder with class head
align image and text features to prototypes
mix prototype supervision with real pairs
post-hoc alignment guided by recycled prototypes

math.words: A simple summary is to score how close an image feature and a text feature are to the same recycled prototype vector, then train the system to increase that shared closeness for matching concepts.
math.equation: score(i, t, c) = sim(v_i, w_c) + sim(u_t, w_c)
symbols: recycled classifier-head weight for class c
a similarity function such as cosine similarity
the joint compatibility of the image and text with prototype c

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an image feature has similarity 0.8 to the dog prototype and the text feature for 'dog' has similarity 0.7 to the same prototype.
If the same image and text each score only 0.2 against the car prototype, the car score is 0.4.
Training pushes matching image-text pairs toward the same prototype and mismatched pairs away from it.

math.note: The real method can be plugged into different aligners, but the shared principle is to use recycled class weights as reference directions.

charts.title: Post-hoc alignment without weight recycling
charts.note: A lightweight aligner without semantic anchors spends more of its limited paired data discovering the basic concept layout from scratch.

charts.title: Weight recycling plus post-hoc alignment
charts.note: The paper reports consistent gains because recycled classifier weights provide concept structure before and during paired training.

items.b: Class heads can encode dataset bias.
items.html: If a class was learned with strong background correlation, its weight vector may capture that bias along with the concept because supervised classification does not guarantee pure semantics.
A class head trained on broad labels may be too coarse for fine-grained text distinctions, so one prototype can collapse several meanings that the text side wants to separate.

items.b: Domain transfer can weaken the anchors.
items.html: If the target images differ sharply from the source classification domain, recycled prototypes may stop being central concept directions because the visual encoder itself has shifted far outside the data range it was trained on.
The method works best when the source classifier learned clean semantic classes and the target alignment task shares enough of that concept inventory to benefit from the recycled anchors.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train a small supervised image classifier on a modest labeled dataset, then freeze its encoder and class head. Build a lightweight image-text aligner with a separate text encoder. Compare two versions: one that discards the class head and one that recycles the class-head weights as semantic prototypes during alignment.

The demo should evaluate zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and few-shot transfer under limited paired data. It should show that the recycled-weight version reaches better alignment earlier because the text encoder has useful concept anchors before many paired examples arrive.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must show that the head weights contribute more than extra learned values. They need to behave as reusable concept structure.
